extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, patent attorneys and agents preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for preparing patent applications, including assessing patentability, meeting disclosure requirements, drafting claims and descriptions, filing/prosecution timing, and documenting inventorship and priority. Geared to practitioners working across multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter (patent eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is patentable subject matter varies by jurisdiction; some technical devices (e.g., an X-ray machine for inspecting structure of bodies) are patentable, while the presentation of information as such (the 'content') is not patentable; a novel and inventive method of presenting information may be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess carefully whether the invention is patent-eligible in the target jurisdiction(s) before pursuing patent protection. If a jurisdiction excludes a category, novelty/inventiveness alone will not secure a patent. Example: a method of generating a 3-D effect icon by arranging colors/brightness may be eligible even if the content itself is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional exclusions from patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subject matter is commonly excluded in many jurisdictions, though exact scope varies: (1) inventions whose commercial exploitation must be prevented to protect public order or morality (including to protect human/animal/plant life or health or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment); (2) diagnostic, therapeutic and surgical methods for the treatment of humans or animals; and (3) plants and animals (other than microorganisms) and essentially biological processes (other than microbiological processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion of treatment methods does not apply to products for use in such treatments (medical products/apparatus/devices may be patentable). In the U.S., methods of treatment are not excluded but patents on such methods cannot be enforced against medical practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In return for exclusive rights, patent holders must sufficiently disclose information about the invention so third parties can learn and avoid duplicative R&D; prevent granting patent rights to subject matter not disclosed or invented before filing; and clearly communicate claim scope so others can avoid infringement or challenge the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure requirements typically include support (written description), enablement, and clarity (definiteness). Some countries additionally require disclosure of the best mode. Once an application is filed, new subject matter generally cannot be added as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement / written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be supported by the description (written description in the U.S.): there must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the scope of the claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is regarded as supported unless a person skilled in the art would be unable, on the basis of the application as filed, to extend the teaching of the description to the whole of the field claimed. U.S. written description: describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a person skilled in the art reasonably concludes the inventor had possession at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely so that a person skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation or inventive effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undue experimentation depends on factors like breadth of claims and predictability of the art. Broader claims may require more extensive disclosure. If the art is predictable and prior art well-known, less detail may be required; unpredictable fields (e.g., new chemical compounds) normally require more detailed instructions on how to produce and the technical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement / definiteness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be clear and concise and distinctly define the subject matter of the invention; vague or indefinite terms are not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most jurisdictions words in a claim get their normal meaning in the relevant art; where appropriate, a drafter may give a word a special defined meaning in the description. Description and drawings may be considered when interpreting claims. See Module VI, section 3 for practical aspects of drafting clear and concise claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries an applicant must indicate in the specification the best mode known to the inventor for carrying out the invention; based on equity to ensure inventors disclose their best way of practicing the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement exists in some jurisdictions but not all. In the United States failure to disclose the best mode is not a ground for cancellation or invalidation of a claim or for holding it unenforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be new; prior publication or disclosure of the invention before filing can cause rejection in many countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what constitutes prior art in the relevant jurisdiction(s). If the invention was published (e.g., academic journal) before filing, this may bar patentability. Use provisional filings and priority rules to manage disclosure timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must involve an inventive step (nonobviousness) beyond the prior art; for determining lack of inventive step, prior art references may be combined to show obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step is distinct from novelty: novelty looks at single references, while inventive step may involve combining references and considering whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability (utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be industrially applicable or useful; industrial applicability/utility is a patentability requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial applicability ensures the invention can be put to practical use. This requirement can present problems for certain fields (e.g., chemical compounds/processes) where demonstrating utility may be challenging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request (application form) contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The request explicitly states that an applicant seeks patent protection and is signed by the applicant or representative; most patent offices supply a specific request form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request form will generally contain: title of the invention; name and address of applicant and representative; indication of inventor(s); and priority claim information (application number and filing date of earlier application). Priority information should be included either on the request form or an application data sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The description discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for a person skilled in the art to carry out the claimed invention and usually contains several sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical elements: (i) title of the invention; (ii) technical field; (iii) background art; (iv) summary of the invention outlining full scope and how problem is solved; (v) brief explanation of the drawings; (vi) detailed disclosure of embodiments with reference to drawings. Embodiments help meet support and enablement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define legal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the scope of exclusive patent protection in terms of technical features; they are the legally operative part of the application and patentability is determined on the basis of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be clear, concise and fully supported by the description. Claims are typically drafted in a particular format (example provided). Drafters commonly prepare claims first as they drive the content of the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings provide visual support and facilitate understanding of the claimed invention; they may include figures, tables, flow charts and diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A representative drawing is often placed on the front page of a published patent document. Use drawings where necessary to understand and exemplify embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract is a summary (digest) of the invention limited to a certain number of words and typically includes key features recited in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primarily an aid for those conducting patent searches and readers of patent documents, delivering an overview of the invention; be concise and reflect claim features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application format and additional required documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications typically include request, description, claims, drawings and abstract; for nucleotide/amino acid sequence inventions a sequence listing may be required; national/regional laws may require additional documents/statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other possible required documents: power of attorney, document of inventor identity, entitlement to apply/grant, oath/declaration of inventorship. Rules vary by jurisdiction—check local requirements carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing timing, priority and time bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Strict rules govern when an application must be filed relative to events such as first public disclosure, attempted commercial exploitation, or export; priority under the Paris Convention and PCT must be claimed within 12 months of the first filing for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask client/inventor when filing is needed and check facts. Public disclosures (publications, presentations, sales, demonstrations, website postings) can create bar dates. Use provisional applications where available as placeholders; docket filing dates and monitor first-anniversary deadlines carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application as a filing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional patent application discloses the invention but does not require claims; it serves as a placeholder and expires one year after filing and can preserve a priority date if a subsequent regular application is filed within one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional filings can rescue situations where an imminent bar date prevents preparation of a full application in time. Draft the best provisional possible within time constraints; ensure adequate disclosure to support later claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention disclosure gathering and interviewing inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain invention disclosures (forms, sketches, reports, prototypes) and interview inventors; position one 'contact inventor' to streamline communications; collect both technical and business information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review disclosures early, note technical and legal questions, and arrange at least one meeting (in person, telephone or video). Do not assume inventors know what constitutes patentable subject matter; the drafter often articulates the patentable concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying patentable inventions (core inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters must focus on patentable aspects within disclosure; inventors may conflate discoveries/products with patentable claimable inventions; the drafter often must articulate the inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore the problem solved in light of prior art to craft essential claim elements. Ask about possible alternatives and embodiments to broaden claim scope. Use examples and follow-up questioning to distinguish inventive features from nonpatentable details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding invention: essential vs non-essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafter should understand invention well enough to define it by the fewest possible elements—know what elements are essential and what need not be recited to obtain the broadest allowable claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm uncertain details with inventors or experts, seek alternative embodiments, and ensure the description discloses working embodiments. The drafter may assist inventors in considering broader applications and alternatives to strengthen disclosure and claim breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications must include the name(s) of the inventor(s); the drafter should ask and confirm who qualifies as inventor(s) since incorrect inventorship can lead to invalidity or unenforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General test: inventor made a creative contribution to the inventive concept. Cultural practices (listing all team members) may differ by country—verify actual inventive contribution. Some jurisdictions limit post-filing amendment of inventorship, so check thoroughly before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing evidence and docketing best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain evidence of filing (mail receipts, electronic confirmations) and docket important dates (e.g., filing date, provisional expiry, priority deadlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing by mail, keep a folder with copies of everything sent and original post office deposit receipt. When filing electronically, save/print the patent office confirmation. Docket the first application filing date and check with applicant well before its first anniversary to preserve foreign filing options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims-first drafting practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drafters ordinarily prepare the claims first because the claims are the heart of a patent and will partly dictate the content of the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the claims to decide what to include in the description and embodiments. Ensure claims are drafted to be as broad as justified by the disclosure while meeting clarity, support and enablement requirements.
